title: NASA discovers massive new crater on the Moon: "Asteroid the size of a six-story building crashed into it"
excerpt: A new crater has been discovered on the Moon: McGetchin, formed by a rare impact in 2024.
content:
The lunar surface continues to change slowly, not because of geological activity, but due to the constant bombardment of asteroids and comet fragments.

The latest example comes from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), which identified a crater formed just two years ago. Named McGetchin, it measures approximately 222 meters in diameter and is the largest recently formed crater discovered in the solar system to date.

A crater that suddenly appeared on the Moon

Between April 11 and May 22, 2024, an asteroid struck the lunar surface; the impact created a crater 222 meters in diameter and 43 meters deep. However, the discovery was made by chance, nearly a year later.

The discovery was made in October 2025 by Robert Wagner, an image-processing specialist for the LROC (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera).

NASA’s robotic Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) has been mapping the Moon from polar orbit since June 2009.

While comparing images of the lunar surface taken at different times in a region near the Moon’s eastern limb, he noticed an unusually bright spot surrounded by a dark halo. Intrigued by the unusual appearance of the impact crater, he compared the image with earlier ones and discovered that the crater had not previously existed.

According to NASA, the impact was caused by an asteroid or comet fragment comparable in size to a three- to six-story building.

The new crater has officially been named McGetchin, in honor of planetary scientist Thomas McGetchin.

McGetchin crater was formed by the impact of an object comparable in size to a three- to six-story building.

It was an extremely rare event: the kind that occurs, on average, only once a century or less frequently.

The impact altered the terrain for several kilometers around the crater

McGetchin crater was photographed by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter both in visible light and with the Diviner radiometer, which can detect thermal anomalies on the lunar surface.

Thermal observations revealed a cold spot around McGetchin: a region spanning between 6 and 7 kilometers that, during the lunar night, registers temperatures up to 8 or 9 Kelvin lower than the surrounding terrain.

The cause is known and is related to the impact and resulting shock wave, which disturbed and loosened the surrounding regolith (the mineral material covering the Moon). This increase in porosity altered the thermal properties of the regolith, causing it to lose heat more quickly after sunset than denser material.

These data show that the effects of a collision can alter the physical characteristics of the terrain at distances many times greater than the size of the resulting crater.

McGetchin gives scientists the opportunity to study a large crater for which detailed images exist from both before and after its formation.

A Moon under constant bombardment

Although the discovery of McGetchin crater is valuable to scientists for the reasons mentioned above, it is not exactly reassuring news. It becomes even less reassuring when considered in the context of lunar impact statistics.

Over more than 17 years of observations by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), astronomers have identified at least 1,000 new craters and approximately 100,000 additional surface changes, linked to impacts or falling ejecta.

According to NASA estimates, around 140 craters large enough to reach roughly 10 meters in diameter form on the Moon each year.

Virtually none of the recent natural lunar craters identified by LRO have been linked to an asteroid that was observed and tracked before impact.

None of the recent natural lunar craters identified by LRO have been linked to an asteroid that was observed and tracked before impact.

The object that created the new McGetchin crater, an asteroid or comet fragment roughly the size of a three- to six-story building, had not been observed before the collision.

This situation highlights the importance of continuing to improve the current system for detecting near-Earth objects (NEOs). Lunar impact statistics reveal how many of these objects continue to go undetected.

It is true that Earth is protected by its atmosphere; friction causes smaller bodies to heat up and disintegrate, eliminating the danger. Nevertheless, even objects the size of three- to six-story buildings can evade our ability to detect them in time.
